<reason>CON (Side A) controlled the decision rule from the start: the motion promises city-wide reductions in deaths and disorder, and a zero count inside a room does not measure that. PRO's replies were competent but kept conceding ground under pressure — a "fraction" of injections captured, a "poisoned supply" everywhere, "enough capacity" needed to avoid overwhelmed sites, and in Latin America that deaths averted are "smaller" while "the second promise does the heavy lifting." CON's second rebuttal and closing weighed those concessions cleanly and turned the disorder promise back into the "fixed queue for armed groups" argument. PRO's rejection of any city-wide metric as a "magic number" was a defensible comparative move but was framed evasively and never gave the judge a test to apply; its late "factory that hands out seatbelts" reframe was answered directly by CON ("a factory needs a door and a nurse, not a supervised chair"), which effectively collapsed PRO's case into CON's cheaper alternative. CON's clipped opening is a minor execution cost, and PRO's dealers-cluster-anyway point kept some life in the disorder clash, but CON made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 1 turning PRO's own "poisoned supply" defense into the case against fixed rooms — if fentanyl kills wherever people use, protection must travel (naloxone, substitution, drug checking), so the room's zero count is beside the point — set up the seatbelt-bolted-to-a-chair image and the concession-based weighing that decided the debate.</best_rebuttal>
